modern: Christians begin to sing in the ways of the Lord when they first lose their burden at the foot of the cross. Not even the songs of the angels seem as sweet as the first song of joy that gushes up from the depths of a forgiven child of God. You know how John Bunyan describes it. He says that when poor Pilgrim lost his burden at the cross, he gave three great leaps and went on his way singing:

Believer, do you remember the day *your* chains fell off? Do you remember the place where Jesus met you and said, “I have loved thee with an everlasting love; I have blotted out as a cloud thy transgressions, and as a thick cloud thy sins; they shall not be mentioned against thee any more for ever.” Oh, what a sweet time that is, when Jesus takes away the pain of sin! When the Lord first pardoned my sin, I was so full of joy I could hardly keep from dancing. On my way home from the place where I had been set free, I thought I had to tell the stones in the street the story of my rescue. My soul was so full of joy that I wanted to tell every snowflake falling from heaven about the wonderful love of Jesus, who had wiped out the sins of one of the worst of rebels.

But it isn’t only at the start of the Christian life that believers have reason to sing. As long as they live, they find reasons to sing in the ways of the Lord, and their experience of his constant lovingkindness leads them to say, “I will bless the Lord at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth.” My friend, make sure you praise the Lord *today*.

notes.note: In John Bunyan’s *The Pilgrim’s Progress*, Christian’s burden falls from his back at the cross and tumbles into the tomb. “Then Christian gave three leaps for joy, and went on singing.” The verse is his song.

modern:
Come, dear readers, let each of us speak for ourselves about the wonderful love, not of Jonathan, but of Jesus. We won’t repeat what we’ve been told, but the things we have tasted and handled of the love of Christ. Your love to me, Jesus, was wonderful when I was a stranger wandering far from you, doing whatever my body and mind desired. Your love held me back from committing the sin that leads to death, and kept me from destroying myself. Your love held back the axe when Justice said, “Cut it down! why cumbereth it the ground?” Your love drew me into the wilderness, stripped me there and made me feel the guilt of my sin and the burden of my wrongdoing. Your love spoke these comforting words to me when I was badly shaken: “Come unto me, and I will give thee rest.”

Oh, how matchless your love was when, in a moment, you washed my sins away! You took my polluted soul, crimson with the blood I was born in and black with the grime of my sins, and made it as white as driven snow and as pure as the finest wool. How you showed your love when you whispered in my ear, “I am thine and thou art mine.” Kind were the words you spoke when you said, “The Father himself loveth you.” And sweet were the moments, sweet beyond words, when you told me of “the love of the Spirit.” My soul will never forget those rooms of fellowship where you have unveiled yourself to me. Did Moses have his cleft in the rock, where he saw the train of God’s glory, the back of his God? We too have had our clefts in the rock, where we’ve seen the full splendor of the Godhead in the person of Christ. Did David remember the tracks of the wild goat, the land of Jordan and the Hermonites? We too can remember places dear to memory, just as blessed as those. Precious Lord Jesus, give us a fresh drink of your wonderful love to start the month with. Amen.

notes.note: David’s lament for his friend Jonathan, killed in battle: “thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women” ([[2Sam.1.26|2 Samuel 1:26]]).

modern: This is the voice of truth that never changes. In none of the Jewish ceremonies were sins taken away, even in picture, without the shedding of blood. In no case, by no means, can sin be pardoned without atonement. So it’s clear that there’s no hope for me outside of Christ, because there’s no other shedding of blood worth a thought as an atonement for sin. Am I, then, believing in him? Has the blood of his atonement really been applied to my soul? Everyone stands on the same level in their need of him. However moral, generous, likable or patriotic we may be, the rule won’t be bent to make an exception for us. Sin will give way to nothing less powerful than the blood of the One God has set forth as a sacrifice for sin. What a blessing that there is the one way of pardon! Why should we look for another?

People whose religion is only a matter of form can’t understand how we can rejoice that all our sins are forgiven for Christ’s sake. Their works and prayers and ceremonies give them very poor comfort. And well may they be uneasy, because they’re neglecting the one great salvation and trying to get forgiveness without blood. My soul, sit down and look at God’s justice, bound to punish sin. See that punishment all carried out on your Lord Jesus, and fall down in humble joy and kiss the dear feet of the One whose blood has made atonement for you. When conscience is awake, it’s useless to run to feelings and evidences for comfort. That’s a habit we learned in the Egypt of our slavery to the law. The only medicine for a guilty conscience is a sight of Jesus suffering on the cross. “The blood is the life thereof,” says the law of Leviticus, and we can be sure it’s the life of faith and joy and every other holy grace.

modern:
Yet not as ancient as the precious things our souls delight in. Let’s count them over for a moment, the way a miser counts his gold. *The Father’s sovereign choice*, by which he chose us for eternal life before the earth existed, is a matter of vast antiquity, because the human mind can’t put a date on it. We were chosen before the foundation of the world. *Everlasting love* went with the choice, because we weren’t set apart by a bare act of God’s will. God’s heart was in it. The Father loved us in and from the beginning. Here is something to think about every day. *The eternal purpose* to rescue us from the ruin he foresaw, to cleanse us and make us holy, and at last to glorify us, is infinitely ancient, and runs side by side with unchanging love and absolute sovereignty. *The covenant* is always described as everlasting, and Jesus, the second party to it, had his goings forth from of old. He shook hands on his sacred pledge to stand for us long before the first star began to shine, and it was in him that the chosen were appointed to eternal life. So in God’s purpose a most blessed covenant union was formed between the Son of God and his chosen people, and it will remain the foundation of their safety when time is no more.

Isn’t it good to know these ancient things well? Isn’t it shameful that so many who call themselves Christians neglect them, and even reject them? If they knew more of their own sin, wouldn’t they be readier to worship the grace that chose them? Let’s both marvel and worship tonight as we sing:

modern:
As God’s creatures, we’re all in debt to him: we owe him obedience with all our body and soul and strength. Having broken his commandments, as we all have, we’re in debt to his justice, and we owe him a vast amount we can’t pay. But it can be said of the *Christian* that they owe God’s *justice* nothing, because Christ has paid the debt his people owed. For that very reason the believer owes all the more to *love*. I’m in debt to God’s grace and forgiving mercy, but I’m not in debt to his justice, because he will never charge me with a debt already paid. Christ said, “It is finished!” and by that he meant that whatever his people owed was wiped out forever from the book of remembrance. Christ has satisfied God’s justice to the full. The account is settled. The handwriting is nailed to the cross. The receipt is given, and we owe God’s justice nothing anymore. But then, because we aren’t in debt to our Lord in that sense, we’re ten times more in debt to God than we would have been otherwise.

Christian, stop and think for a moment. What a debtor you are to God’s *sovereignty*! How much you owe to his unselfish love, for he gave his own Son to die for you. Think how much you owe to his forgiving *grace*: after ten thousand insults he loves you as infinitely as ever. Think what you owe to his *power*: how he has raised you from your death in sin, how he has kept your spiritual life going, how he has kept you from falling, and how, though a thousand enemies have blocked your path, you’ve been able to keep on your way. Think what you owe to his *unchangingness*. Though you’ve changed a thousand times, he hasn’t changed once. You’re as deep in debt as you can be to every quality of God. You owe God yourself and everything you have. Give yourself as a living sacrifice; it’s only your reasonable service.

notes.note: God’s record ([[Mal.3.16|Malachi 3:16]]); here, the record of our debts.

modern:
These words express the believer’s desire for Christ, their longing for fellowship with him now. Where do you feed your flock? In *your house*? I’ll go, if I can find you there. In private *prayer*? Then I’ll pray without ceasing. In the *Word*? Then I’ll read it carefully. In your *ordinances*? Then I’ll walk in them with all my heart. Tell me where you feed your flock, because wherever you stand as the Shepherd, there I’ll lie down as a sheep, since no one but you can supply what I need. I can’t be content to be apart from you. My soul hungers and thirsts for the refreshment of your presence. “Where dost thou make thy flock to rest at noon?” Whether at dawn or at noon, my only rest must be where you and your beloved flock are. My soul’s rest must be a rest given by grace, and it can only be found in you. Where is the shadow of that rock? Why shouldn’t I rest under it? “Why should I be as one that turneth aside by the flocks of thy companions?” You have companions; why shouldn’t I be one?

Satan tells me I’m unworthy. But I always was unworthy, and yet you’ve loved me for a long time, so my unworthiness can’t stop me having fellowship with you now. It’s true I’m weak in faith and quick to fall, but my very weakness is the reason I should always be where you feed your flock, so that I can be made strong and kept safe beside the still waters. Why should I turn aside? There’s no reason I should, but there are a thousand reasons I shouldn’t, because Jesus is calling me to come. If he has drawn back a little, it’s only to make me value his presence more. Now that I’m grieved and upset at being away from him, he’ll lead me once again to that sheltered corner where the lambs of his flock are shaded from the burning sun.

modern:
Believer, *look back* over all your experience. Think of the way the Lord your God has led you in the wilderness, and how he has fed and clothed you every day. Think how he has put up with your bad manners, with all your grumbling and all your longings for the meat pots of Egypt. Think how he has opened the rock to supply you, and fed you with manna that came down from heaven. Think how his grace has been enough for you in all your troubles, how his blood has pardoned you for all your sins, how his rod and his staff have comforted you.

When you’ve looked back like this on the love of the Lord, then let faith look ahead at his love *in the future*. Remember that Christ’s covenant and blood hold more than the *past*. The One who has loved you and pardoned you will never stop loving and pardoning. He is the Alpha, and he will be the Omega too: he is first, and he will be *last*. So think: when you pass through the valley of the shadow of death, you won’t need to fear any evil, because he is with you. When you stand in the cold floods of Jordan, you won’t need to be afraid, because death can’t separate you from his love. And when you come into the mysteries of eternity, you won’t need to tremble, “For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

Now, my soul, isn’t your love refreshed? Doesn’t this make you love Jesus? Doesn’t a flight across the endless skies of love set your heart on fire and make you delight yourself in the Lord your God? Surely as we think about “the love of the Lord,” our hearts burn within us, and we long to love him more.

modern:
It’s said that in the land of Canaan the cities of refuge were placed so that anyone could reach one within half a day at most. In the same way, the word of our salvation is close to us. Jesus is a Savior here and now, and the way to him is short. It’s simply giving up trust in our own merit and taking hold of Jesus to be our all in all. We’re told that the roads to the cities of refuge were carefully kept up. Every river was bridged and every obstacle removed, so that the man running for his life could get through easily to the city. Once a year the elders went along the roads and checked them, so that nothing would hold up anyone fleeing and make him get caught and killed. How graciously the promises of the gospel clear stumbling blocks out of the way! Wherever there were side roads and turnings, signposts were put up with the words “To the city of refuge!” This is a picture of the road to Christ Jesus. It isn’t the long way around of the law. It isn’t obeying this, that and the other. It’s a straight road: “Believe, and live.” It’s a road so hard that no self-righteous person can ever walk it, but so easy that every sinner who knows they’re a sinner can find their way to heaven by it.

The moment the man who had killed someone reached the outer edge of the city, he was safe. He didn’t need to go far inside the walls; the outskirts themselves were protection enough. Learn from this that if you only touch the hem of Christ’s garment, you’ll be made well. If you only take hold of him with “faith as a grain of mustard seed,” you’re safe.
Only don’t waste time or dawdle on the way, because the avenger of blood is fast on his feet, and he may be right at your heels at this quiet evening hour.

modern:
It’s a sweet thought that Jesus Christ didn’t come out without his Father’s permission, authority, agreement and help. He was sent by the Father to be the Savior of men. We’re too quick to forget that while there are distinctions between the *persons* of the Trinity, there are no distinctions of *honor*. Too often we give the honor for our salvation, or at least for the depth of its kindness, more to Jesus Christ than to the Father. That’s a very great mistake. So what if Jesus came? Didn’t his Father send him? If he spoke wonderfully, didn’t his Father pour grace into his lips, so that he could be an able minister of the new covenant? Anyone who knows the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit as they should never puts one ahead of another in their love. They see them at Bethlehem, at Gethsemane and on Calvary, all equally at work in salvation.

Christian, have you put your confidence in the Man Christ Jesus? Have you placed your trust in him alone? And are you united with him? Then believe that you’re united with the God of heaven. Since you’re a brother or sister to the Man Christ Jesus, and have the closest fellowship with him, you’re linked through him with the eternal God, and “the Ancient of days” is your Father and your friend. Have you ever thought about the depth of love in the heart of the Lord when God the Father equipped his Son for the great mission of mercy? If not, make it your meditation today. The *Father* sent him! Think about that. Think how Jesus does what the *Father* wills. In the wounds of the dying Savior, see the love of the great I AM. Let every thought of Jesus also be tied to the eternal, ever-blessed God, for “It pleased the Lord to bruise him; he hath put him to grief.”

modern:
This is an unusual way to start a verse: “At that time Jesus answered.” If you look at what comes before, you won’t see that anyone had asked him a question, or that he was talking with anyone at all. Yet it’s written, “Jesus answered and said, I thank thee, O Father.” When someone answers, they answer a person who has been speaking to them. So who had spoken to Christ? His Father. Yet there’s no record of it, and this should teach us that Jesus had constant fellowship with his Father. God spoke into his heart so often, so continually, that it wasn’t unusual enough to be written down. Talking with God was the habit and life of Jesus.

As Jesus was in this world, so are we. So let’s learn the lesson this simple statement about him teaches. May we also have silent fellowship with the Father, so that we often answer him. And though the world doesn’t know who we’re talking to, may we be answering that secret voice no other ear hears, which our own ear, opened by the Spirit of God, recognizes with joy. God has spoken to us, so let’s speak to God: to put our seal on it that God is true and faithful to his promise, or to confess the sin the Spirit of God has shown us, or to thank him for the mercy his providence has given, or to say yes to the great truths the Holy Spirit has opened to our understanding.

What a privilege close fellowship with the Father of our spirits is! It’s a secret hidden from the world, a joy not even our closest friend can share in. If we want to hear the whispers of God’s love, our ear must be cleansed and made ready to listen to his voice. This very evening, may our hearts be in such a state that when God speaks to us, we, like Jesus, are ready at once to answer him.

modern:
What a multitude of prayers we’ve sent up since we first learned to pray! Our first prayer was for ourselves. We asked God to have mercy on us and wipe out our sin, and he heard us. But once he had wiped out our sins like a cloud, we had more prayers for ourselves. We’ve had to pray for grace to make us holy, for grace to move us and grace to hold us back. We’ve been led to beg for fresh assurance of faith, for the comfort of the promise brought home to us, for rescue in the hour of temptation, for help in the time of duty and for support in the day of trial. We’ve had to go to God for our souls like constant beggars, asking for everything. Bear witness, children of God: you’ve never been able to get anything for your souls anywhere else. All the bread your soul has eaten has come down from heaven, and all the water it has drunk has flowed from the living rock, Christ Jesus the Lord. Your soul has never grown rich in itself. It has always lived on God’s daily generosity, and so your prayers have gone up to heaven for an almost endless range of spiritual mercies. Your needs were countless, so the supplies have been infinitely great, and your prayers have been as varied as the mercies have been countless.

So don’t you have reason to say, “I love the Lord, because he hath heard the voice of my supplication”? Because as your prayers have been many, so have God’s answers to them. He has heard you in the day of trouble, strengthened you and helped you, even when you dishonored him by trembling and doubting at the mercy seat. Remember this, and let it fill your heart with gratitude to God, who has so graciously heard your poor, weak prayers. “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits.”

notes.note: Grace that urges us on to good, and grace that holds us back from evil.

modern:
To encourage you to pray gladly for others, remember that *prayer like this is the sweetest God ever hears*, because Christ’s prayer is of this kind. In all the incense our great High Priest now puts in the golden censer, there’s not a single grain for himself. His intercession must be the most welcome of all prayers, and the more our prayer is like Christ’s, the sweeter it will be. So while our requests for ourselves will be accepted, our pleading for others, which has more of the fruit of the Spirit in it, more love, more faith, more brotherly kindness, will be the sweetest offering we can bring to God through the precious merits of Jesus, the very fat of our sacrifice.

Remember too that *praying for others is extremely powerful*. What wonders it has done! The Word of God is full of its marvelous deeds. Believer, you have a mighty engine in your hand. Use it well, use it constantly, use it in faith, and you’ll surely be a blessing to your brothers and sisters. When you have the King’s ear, speak to him for the suffering members of his body. When you’re given the favor of coming very near his throne, and the King says to you, “Ask, and I will give thee what thou wilt,” don’t ask for yourself alone, but for the many who need his help. If you have grace at all and don’t pray for others, that grace must be as small as a grain of mustard seed. You have just enough grace to float your soul clear of the quicksand, but no deep floods of grace, or else you’d carry a heavy cargo of other people’s needs in your happy boat, and bring back from your Lord rich blessings for them that they might not have received without you:

modern:
The hour is coming when the message will come to us, as it comes to everyone: “Arise, and leave the home you’ve lived in, the city where you’ve done your business, your family and your friends. Arise, and take your last journey.” And what do we know about the journey? What do we know about the country we’re headed for? We’ve read a little about it, and the Spirit has shown us something of it. But how little we know of the world to come! We know there’s a dark and stormy river called “Death.” God tells us to cross it, and promises to be with us. And after death, what comes? What wonder-world will open before our astonished eyes? What scene of glory will unfold in front of us? No traveler has ever come back to tell. But we know enough about the heavenly land to welcome our summons there with joy and gladness.

The journey of death may be dark, but we can set out on it without fear, knowing that God is with us as we walk through the gloomy valley, so we don’t need to fear any evil. We’ll be leaving everything we’ve known and loved here, but we’ll be going to our Father’s house, our Father’s home, where Jesus is, to that royal “city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.” This will be our last move, to live forever with the One we love, among his people, in the presence of God. Christian, think much about heaven. It will help you keep going and forget the hard work of the road. This valley of tears is only the path to the better country. This world of sorrow is only the stepping stone to a world of joy.

modern: Leaving aside what these words mean in their setting in the prophecy, let’s take them as our great Forerunner’s invitation to his holy people. In due time every believer will hear “a great voice from heaven” saying, “Come up hither.” For God’s people this should be *something to look forward to with joy*. Instead of dreading the time when we’ll leave this world to go to the Father, we should be longing for the hour we’re set free. Our song should be:

We aren’t called down to the grave, but up to the skies. Our spirits, born from heaven, should long for their native air. Yet we should also *wait patiently* for the heavenly summons. Our God knows best when to say to us, “Come up hither.” We mustn’t wish to bring forward the time of our departure. I know strong love will make us cry,

but patience must have her perfect work. God appoints with exact wisdom the best time for the redeemed to stay here below. Surely, if there could be regrets in heaven, the saints might be sorry they didn’t live longer here to do more good. Oh, for more sheaves for my Lord’s barn! More jewels for his crown! But how, unless there’s more work? True, there’s the other side of it: living so short a time, we sin less. But oh, when we’re fully serving God, and he’s giving us precious seed to scatter and a hundredfold harvest to reap, we’d even say it’s good for us to stay where we are. Whether our Master says “go” or “stay,” let’s be equally pleased, as long as he blesses us with his presence.

modern:
When someone is dear to us, everything connected with them becomes dear for their sake. In the same way, the person of the Lord Jesus is so precious to all true believers that they count everything about him priceless. “All thy garments smell of myrrh, and aloes, and cassia,” said David, as if the Savior’s very clothes were so sweetened by his person that he couldn’t help loving them. It’s certain that there isn’t a place that holy foot has walked, not a word those blessed lips have spoken, not a thought his loving Word has revealed, that isn’t priceless to us. And this is true of the *names* of Christ: they’re all sweet to a believer’s ear. Whether he’s called the Husband of the church, her Bridegroom, her Friend; whether he’s named the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, the King, the Prophet or the Priest; every title of our Master, Shiloh, Emmanuel, Wonderful, the Mighty Counselor, every name is like a honeycomb dripping with honey, and sweet are the drops that fall from it.

But if there’s one name sweeter than the rest to a believer’s ear, it’s the name of *Jesus*. Jesus! It’s the name that stirs the harps of heaven to music. Jesus! The life of all our joys. If there’s one name more delightful, more precious than any other, it’s this one. It’s woven into the very fabric of our hymns. Many of our hymns begin with it, and hardly any that are good for anything end without it. It’s the sum total of every delight. It’s the music the bells of heaven ring, a song in a word, an ocean in its meaning though a drop in its length, a matchless oratorio in two syllables, all the hallelujahs of eternity gathered up in five letters.

modern:
If you ask many people what they understand by salvation, they’ll answer, “Being saved from hell and taken to heaven.” That is one result of salvation, but it isn’t a tenth of what that gift contains. It’s true that our Lord Jesus Christ rescues all his people from the wrath to come. He saves them from the terrible condemnation their sins had brought on them. But his triumph is far more complete than that. He saves his people “from their sins.” Oh, what a sweet rescue from our worst enemies! Wherever Christ does his saving work, he throws Satan off his throne and won’t let him be master any longer. No one is a true Christian if sin rules in their mortal body. Sin will be in us. It will never be completely driven out until the spirit enters glory. But it will never have *dominion*. There will be a struggle for control, a pulling against the new law and the new spirit God has planted in us, but sin will never get the upper hand and become absolute ruler of our nature. Christ will be Master of the heart, and sin must be put to death. The Lion of the tribe of Judah will win, and the dragon will be thrown out.

You who claim to be a Christian: has sin been brought under in you? If your *life* is unholy, your *heart* is unchanged, and if your heart is unchanged, you aren’t saved. If the Savior hasn’t made you holy, made you new, given you a hatred of sin and a love of holiness, he hasn’t done anything saving in you. Grace that doesn’t make someone better than others is a worthless fake. Christ saves his people, not in their sins, but *from* them. “Without holiness no man shall see the Lord.” “Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.” If we aren’t saved from sin, how can we hope to be counted among his people? Lord, save me now from all evil, and help me honor my Savior.

modern:
When David asked this, he had just fought the Philistines and won a remarkable victory. The Philistines had come up in great armies, but with God’s help David had easily put them to flight. Notice, though, that when they came a second time, David didn’t go up to fight them without asking the Lord. He’d won once, and he could have said, as many have in other cases, “I’ll win again. I can be quite sure that if I’ve won once, I’ll win again. Why should I wait around to ask the Lord?” Not David. He had won one battle by the Lord’s strength, and he wouldn’t risk another until he was sure of the same. He asked, “Shall I go up against them?” He waited until God gave his sign.

Learn from David to take no step without God. Christian, if you want to know the path of duty, take God as your compass. If you want to steer your ship through the dark waves, put the tiller in the Almighty’s hand. We could escape many a rock if we let our Father take the helm. We could avoid many a sandbank or quicksand if we left it to his sovereign will to choose and command. The Puritan said, “As sure as ever a Christian carves for himself, he’ll cut his own fingers;” and that’s very true. Another old preacher said, “He that goes before the cloud of God’s providence goes on a fool’s errand;” and so he does. We must watch for God’s providence leading us, and if providence waits, we must wait until it comes. Anyone who runs ahead of providence will be very glad to run back again. “I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go,” is God’s promise to his people. So let’s take all our puzzles to him and say, “Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?” Don’t leave your room this morning without asking the Lord.

modern: What we’re taught to seek or avoid in prayer, we should seek or avoid just as much in action. So we should take great care to avoid temptation, walking so carefully in the path of obedience that we never tempt the devil to tempt us. We aren’t to go into the thicket looking for the lion. We might pay dearly for that kind of presumption. The lion may cross our path or spring at us from the thicket, but we have no business hunting him. Whoever meets him, even if he wins the day, will find it a hard struggle. Let the Christian pray to be spared the encounter. Our Savior, who knew from experience what temptation meant, earnestly warned his disciples, “Pray that ye enter not into temptation.”

But whatever we do, we’ll be tempted, and so we pray, “deliver us from evil.” God had one Son without sin, but he has no son without temptation. The natural man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward, and the Christian is born to temptation just as surely. We must always be on watch against Satan, because, like a thief, he gives no warning that he’s coming. Believers who have learned Satan’s ways know there are certain times when he’s most likely to attack, just as bitter winds can be expected at certain seasons. So the Christian is put doubly on guard by the fear of danger, and the danger is turned away by getting ready to meet it. Prevention is better than cure. It’s better to be so well armed that the devil won’t attack you than to go through the dangers of the fight, even if you come out the winner. This evening, pray first that you won’t be tempted, and then that if temptation is allowed, you’ll be rescued from the evil one.

modern:
There are many who know “how to be abased” who haven’t learned “how to abound.” When they’re set on a high pinnacle, their heads spin and they’re ready to fall. Christians far more often disgrace what they profess in good times than in bad. It’s a dangerous thing to prosper. The crucible of hardship is a lighter test for a Christian than the refining pot of prosperity. Oh, what thinness of soul and neglect of spiritual things God’s very mercies and gifts have brought on! Yet it doesn’t have to be that way, because the apostle tells us he knew how to abound. When he had much, he knew how to use it. Abundant grace let him handle abundant prosperity. When his sails were full, he carried plenty of ballast, and so he stayed safely afloat. It takes more than human skill to carry the brimming cup of earthly joy with a steady hand, yet Paul had learned that skill, for he says, “In all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry.”

Knowing how to be full is a lesson only God can teach. The Israelites were full once, but while the meat was still in their mouths, God’s anger came on them. Many have asked for mercies so they could satisfy their own hearts’ desires. Plenty of bread has often meant plenty of hot blood, and that has led to an unruly spirit. When we have a lot of God’s mercies in this life, we often have little of God’s grace, and little gratitude for the gifts we’ve received. We’re full, and we forget God. Satisfied with earth, we’re content to do without heaven. You can be sure it’s harder to know how to be full than how to be hungry, because human nature leans so desperately toward pride and forgetting God. Make sure you ask God in your prayers to teach you “how to be full.”

modern: Look carefully at *the instructive comparison*: our sins are like a *cloud*. As clouds come in many shapes and shades, so do our sins. As clouds hide the light of the sun and darken the land below, so our sins hide the light of God’s face from us and make us sit in the shadow of death. They’re earthborn things that rise from the swampy places of our nature, and when they’ve gathered to their full measure, they threaten us with storm and tempest. Sadly, unlike clouds, our sins give us no gentle showers, but threaten to drown us in a fiery flood of destruction. You black clouds of sin, how can there be fair weather in our souls while you’re still here?

Let our eyes rest with joy on *the remarkable act* of God’s mercy: “blotting out.” God himself appears on the scene, and in his divine kindness, instead of showing his anger, he reveals his grace. He removes the trouble at once and forever, not by blowing the cloud away, but by blotting it out of existence once for all. No sin remains against the one God has declared righteous. The great transaction of the cross has taken their sins away forever. On the top of Calvary the great deed that put away the sin of all the chosen forever was completely and effectively done.

In practice, let’s obey *the gracious command*: “*return unto me*.” Why should pardoned sinners live far away from their God? If we’ve been forgiven all our sins, let’s not let any fear of the law keep us from coming boldly to our Lord. Let’s grieve over our backslidings, but let’s not keep on in them. In the power of the Holy Spirit, let’s struggle hard to come back to the closest possible fellowship with the Lord. O Lord, bring us back tonight!

modern:
A Christian should be a striking likeness of Jesus Christ. You’ve read lives of Christ, beautifully and eloquently written, but the best life of Christ is his living biography, written out in the words and actions of his people. If we were what we claim to be, and what we should be, we’d be pictures of Christ. Yes, we’d be such striking likenesses of him that the world wouldn’t have to hold us up and study us for an hour and then say, “Well, there’s something of a likeness.” As soon as they saw us they’d exclaim, “He’s been with Jesus. Jesus has taught him. He’s like him. He has caught the very idea of the holy Man of Nazareth, and he works it out in his life and everyday actions.”

A Christian should be like Christ in his *boldness*. Never blush to admit your faith. What you profess will never disgrace you; take care you never disgrace *it*. Be like Jesus, very brave for your God. Copy his *loving* spirit. Think kindly, speak kindly and act kindly, so that people will say of you, “He has been with Jesus.” Copy Jesus in his *holiness*. Was he zealous for his Master? Then be zealous too, always going about doing good. Don’t waste time; it’s too precious. Was he self-denying, never looking out for himself? Be the same. Was he devout? Be earnest in your prayers. Did he yield to his Father’s will? Then submit yourself to him. Was he patient? Then learn to endure. And best of all, as the highest likeness of Jesus, try to forgive your enemies as he did, and let those sublime words of your Master, “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do,” always ring in your ears. Forgive as you hope to be forgiven. Heap coals of fire on your enemy’s head by your kindness to him. Good for evil, remember, is godlike. So be godlike, and in every way and by every means, live so that everyone will say of you, “He has been with Jesus.”

modern:
That best and brightest of hours is always to be remembered: when we first saw the Lord, lost our burden, received the scroll of promise, rejoiced in full salvation and went on our way in peace. It was springtime in the soul. The winter was past. The rumbling of Sinai’s thunder had gone quiet, and its lightning flashes were seen no more. We saw that God was at peace with us. The law threatened no vengeance, and justice demanded no punishment. Then flowers appeared in our hearts. Hope, love, peace and patience sprang up from the soil. The hyacinth of repentance, the snowdrop of pure holiness, the crocus of golden faith, the daffodil of early love all decorated the garden of the soul. The time of the singing of birds had come, and we rejoiced with thanksgiving. We praised the holy name of our forgiving God, and our resolve was, “Lord, I’m yours, wholly yours. All I am and all I have, I want to give to you. You bought me with your blood; let me spend myself and be spent in your service. In life and in death, let me be given over to you.”

*How have we kept that resolve?* Our first love burned with a holy flame of devotion to Jesus. Is it the same *now*? Couldn’t Jesus well say to us, “I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love”? Sadly, we’ve done very little for our Master’s glory. Our winter has lasted far too long. We’re as cold as ice when we should feel a summer’s warmth and bloom with holy flowers. We give God pennies when he deserves pounds; no, when he deserves to have our heart’s blood minted into coin for the service of his church and his truth. But are we going to go on like this? O Lord, after you’ve blessed us so richly, are we going to be ungrateful and grow careless about your good cause and work? Oh, bring us back to life, so that we may return to our first love and do our first works! Send us a warm spring, O Sun of Righteousness.

modern:
There’s a blessed balance here. The Ruler of providence holds a pair of scales. On one side he puts his people’s trials, and on the other their comforts. When the scale of trials is nearly empty, you’ll always find the scale of comfort in much the same state. And when the scale of trials is full, you’ll find the scale of comfort just as heavy. When the black clouds gather thickest, the light shines out to us all the brighter. When the night darkens and the storm is coming on, the heavenly Captain is always closest to his crew. It’s a blessed thing that when we’re most cast down, that’s when we’re most lifted up by the comforts of the Spirit.

One reason is that *trials make more room for comfort*. Great hearts can only be made by great troubles. The spade of trouble digs the reservoir of comfort deeper and makes more room for consolation. God comes into our heart and finds it full. He begins to break our comforts and empty it, and then there’s more room for grace. The lower a person lies, the more comfort they’ll always have, because they’ll be better fitted to receive it.

Another reason we’re often happiest in our troubles is that *then we have the closest dealings with God*. When the barn is full, people can live without God. When the purse is bursting with gold, we try to get by with less prayer. But take our *gourds* away, and we want our *God*. Clear the idols out of the house, and then we’re forced to honor the Lord. “Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O Lord.” No cry is as good as the one that comes from the bottom of the mountains. No prayer is half as heartfelt as the one that comes up from the depths of the soul through deep trials and troubles. So trials bring us to God, and we’re happier, because nearness to God is happiness. Come, troubled believer, don’t fret over your heavy troubles, because they’re the heralds of weighty mercies.

modern:
The great Father revealed himself to believers long ago, before his Son came, and was known to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as God Almighty. Then Jesus came, and the ever-blessed Son in his own person was the delight of his people’s eyes. When the Redeemer ascended, the Holy Spirit became head of the present age, and his power was gloriously shown at and after Pentecost. He remains at this very hour the present Immanuel, God with us, living in and with his people, giving life, guiding and ruling among them. Is his presence recognized as it ought to be? We can’t control his working. He is entirely sovereign in all he does. But are we eager enough to have his help, or careful enough not to provoke him to withdraw it? Without him we can do nothing, but by his almighty power the most extraordinary results can come about. Everything depends on whether he shows or hides his power.

Do we always look to him, for our inner life and our outward service, with the respectful dependence that’s fitting? Don’t we too often run ahead of his call and act without his help? Let’s humble ourselves this evening for our past neglect, and now beg for the heavenly dew to rest on us, the holy oil to anoint us, the heavenly flame to burn within us. The Holy Spirit is no passing gift. He stays with God’s people. We only have to seek him in the right way, and we’ll find him. He is jealous, but he is full of pity. If he leaves in anger, he comes back in mercy. Humble and tender, he doesn’t grow tired of us, but still waits to be gracious.

modern:
“Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us.” Think about who we were, and what we feel ourselves to be even now, when sin is still strong in us, and you’ll be amazed that we’ve been adopted. Yet we’re called “*the sons of God*.” What a high relationship it is to be a son, and what privileges it brings! What care and tenderness a son expects from his father, and what love the father feels for his son! But we have all *that*, and more, through Christ now. As for the passing drawback of suffering along with our elder brother, we accept it as an honor: “Therefore the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not.” We’re content to be unknown with him in his humiliation, because we’re going to be lifted up with him.

“*Beloved, now are we the sons of God*.” That’s easy to read, but not so easy to feel. How is it with your heart this morning? Are you in the lowest depths of sorrow? Is sin rising up in your spirit, and does grace seem like a poor spark trampled underfoot? Is your faith almost failing? Don’t be afraid. You aren’t meant to live on your graces or your feelings. You must live simply by faith in Christ. With all these things against us, now, in the very depths of our sorrow, wherever we may be, *now*, as much in the valley as on the mountain, “Beloved, *now* are we the sons of God.” “Ah, but,” you say, “look how I’m dressed! My graces aren’t bright. My righteousness doesn’t shine with any glory anyone can see.” But read what comes next: *“It doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him.”* The Holy Spirit will purify our minds, and God’s power will refine our bodies, and then *we shall see him as he is*.

modern:
Come, my soul, think about this. Believing in Jesus, you’re actually and effectively cleared of guilt. You’ve been led out of your prison. You’re no longer in chains like a slave. You’ve been set free *now* from slavery to the law. You’ve been freed from sin, and you can walk around as a free person. Your Savior’s blood has bought your full discharge. You have the right now to come to your Father’s throne. There are no flames of vengeance there to frighten you now, no fiery sword. Justice can’t strike the innocent. Everything that barred you has been taken away. Once you couldn’t see your Father’s face; you can see it now. You couldn’t speak with him, but now you can come to him boldly. Once the fear of hell hung over you, but you don’t fear it now, because how can there be punishment for those who aren’t guilty? Whoever believes isn’t condemned and can’t be punished.

And more than all that, the privileges you might have enjoyed if you had never sinned are yours now that you’ve been justified. All the blessings you would have had if you had kept the law, and more, are yours, because Christ has kept it for you. All the love and acceptance that perfect obedience could have won from God belong to you, because Christ was perfectly obedient for you and has credited all his merits to your account, so that you might be exceedingly rich through him who for your sake became exceedingly poor. Oh, how great a debt of love and gratitude you owe your Savior!

modern: Jehoiachin wasn’t sent away from the king’s palace with supplies to last him for months. His food was given to him as a daily allowance. In this he’s a good picture of the happy position of all the Lord’s people. A daily share is *all anyone really needs*. We don’t need tomorrow’s supplies. That day hasn’t dawned yet, and its needs haven’t been born. The thirst we may feel in June doesn’t need to be quenched in February, because we don’t feel it yet. If we have enough for each day as the days come, we’ll never be in want. Enough for the day is *all we can enjoy*. We can’t eat or drink or wear more than the day’s supply of food and clothes. Anything extra just gives us the worry of storing it and the anxiety of guarding it against thieves. One walking stick helps a traveler, but a bundle of sticks is a heavy load. Enough isn’t only as good as a feast; it’s all the greatest glutton can really enjoy. This is *all we should expect*. Craving more than this is ungrateful. When our Father doesn’t give us more, we should be content with his daily allowance. Jehoiachin’s case is ours. We have a sure share, a share *given us by the King*, a *gracious* share, and a *never-ending* share. Here, surely, is reason to be thankful.

Dear Christian reader, when it comes to grace, *you need a daily supply*. You have no stockpile of strength. Day by day you must look for help from above. It’s a very sweet assurance that *a daily share is provided for you*. In the Word, through preaching, by meditation, in prayer and in waiting on God, you’ll receive fresh strength. Everything you need is stored up for you in Jesus. So *enjoy your continual allowance*. Never go hungry while the daily bread of grace is on the table of mercy.

modern:
Here tonight is one of the most touching and instructive of the Savior’s miracles. The woman knew very little. She imagined that power flowed out of Christ automatically, like a law of nature, without his knowing or choosing it. She also didn’t know how generous Jesus is, or she wouldn’t have crept up behind him to steal the cure he was so ready to give. Misery should always put itself right in front of mercy. If she had known the love of Jesus’ heart, she would have said, “I only have to put myself where he can see me. He knows everything, so he’ll know my case, and his love will heal me at once.” We admire her faith, but we’re amazed at how little she knew.

After she had been healed, she rejoiced with trembling. She was glad that God’s power had done a wonder in her, but she was afraid Christ might take the blessing back and cancel the gift of his grace. How little she understood the fullness of his love! We don’t see him as clearly as we’d like. We don’t know the heights and depths of his love. But we know for certain that he’s too good to take back from a trembling soul the gift it has managed to receive.

But here’s the marvel of it: little as she knew, her faith, because it was real faith, saved her, and saved her at once. There was no long delay. Faith’s miracle was instant. If we have faith as small as a mustard seed, salvation is ours, now and forever. If we’re listed among the Lord’s children as the weakest of the family, we’re still heirs through faith, and no power, human or devilish, can throw us out of salvation. If we don’t dare to lean our heads on his chest like John, but can still slip through the crowd behind him and touch the hem of his garment, we’re made whole. Courage, timid one! Your faith has saved you; go in peace. “*Being* justified by faith, we *have* peace with God.”

modern:
Heaven will be full of the never-ending praises of Jesus. Eternity, your countless years will race along their everlasting course, but forever and ever, “to him be glory.” Isn’t he “a Priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek”? “To him be glory.” Isn’t he King forever, King of kings and Lord of lords, the everlasting Father? “To him be glory *for ever*.” His praises will never stop. What was bought with blood deserves to last as long as immortality lasts. The glory of the cross must never be eclipsed; the brightness of the grave and the resurrection must never be dimmed. O Jesus, you’ll be praised forever! As long as undying spirits live, as long as the Father’s throne stands, forever and ever, glory will be yours.

Believer, you’re looking forward to the time when you’ll join the saints above in giving all the glory to Jesus. But are you glorifying him *now*? The apostle’s words are, “To him be glory both now and for ever.” Won’t you make it your prayer today? “Lord, help me to glorify you. I’m poor; help me to glorify you by being content. I’m sick; help me to honor you by being patient. I have talents; help me to praise you by spending them for you. I have time; Lord, help me to make the most of it, so that I can serve you. I have a heart to feel; Lord, let that heart feel no love but yours, and glow with no flame but love for you. I have a head to think; Lord, help me to think *of* you and *for* you. You’ve put me in this world for something; Lord, show me what it is, and help me to work out my life’s purpose. I can’t do much, but as the widow put in her two small coins, which were all she had to live on, so, Lord, I throw my time and my eternity too into your treasury. I’m all yours. Take me, and help me to glorify you *now*, in all I say, in all I do, and with all I have.”

modern:
And who has the privilege of making the Savior glad like this? His church, his people. But is it possible? He makes *us* glad, but how can *we make him glad*? By our love. Ah, we think it’s so cold, so faint, and sadly we have to admit it is. But it’s very sweet to Christ. Listen to his own praise of that love in the golden Song: “How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine!” See, loving heart, how he delights in you. When you lean your head on his chest, you don’t only receive joy; you give him joy. When you gaze lovingly at his all-glorious face, you don’t only get comfort; you give him delight. Our *praise* gives him joy too: not just the song of our lips, but the music of our heart’s deep gratitude. Our *gifts* are very pleasing to him as well. He loves to see us lay our time, our talents and our money on the altar, not for the value of what we give, but for the sake of the love behind it. To him the humble offerings of his people are more welcome than thousands of gold and silver coins.

*Holiness* is like frankincense and myrrh to him. Forgive your enemy, and you make Christ glad. Share your money with the poor, and he rejoices. Be the means of saving souls, and you let him see the fruit of his soul’s labor. Preach his gospel, and you’re a sweet fragrance to him. Go among people who don’t know him and lift up the cross, and you’ve honored him. It’s in your power even now to break the alabaster jar and pour the precious oil of joy on his head, as the woman did long ago, whose story is still told wherever the gospel is preached. Will you hang back, then? Won’t you perfume your beloved Lord with the myrrh and aloes and cassia of your heart’s praise? Yes, you ivory palaces, you’ll hear the songs of the saints!

modern:
These words show us that contentment doesn’t come naturally to human beings. “Ill weeds grow apace.” Greed, discontent and grumbling are as natural to us as thorns are to the soil. We don’t need to sow thistles and brambles. They come up naturally enough, because they’re native to the earth. In the same way, we don’t need to teach people to complain. They complain fast enough without any education. But the precious things of the earth have to be cultivated. If we want wheat, we have to plow and sow. If we want flowers, there must be a garden and all the gardener’s care. Contentment is one of the flowers of heaven, and if we want it, it has to be cultivated. It won’t grow in us by nature. Only the new nature can produce it, and even then we must take special care and keep watch to tend the grace God has sown in us.

Paul says, “I have *learned*… to be content,” as much as to say that once he didn’t know how. It cost him some pains to grasp the secret of that great truth. No doubt there were times he thought he had learned it, and then broke down. And when at last he had it, and could say, “I have learned in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content,” he was an old, gray-haired man near the edge of the grave, a poor prisoner shut up in Nero’s dungeon at Rome. We might well be willing to bear Paul’s weaknesses and share his cold dungeon, if we too could somehow reach his level. Don’t imagine that you can be content without *learning* it, or learn it without discipline. It isn’t a power that comes naturally, but a skill acquired gradually. We know this from experience. My friend, hush that grumble, natural as it is, and keep on as a hardworking student in the College of Contentment.

modern:
The sin of forgetting the Holy Spirit is common, far too common. It’s foolish and ungrateful. He deserves well from us, because he is good, supremely good. As God, he is good *in his very nature*. He shares in the threefold cry of “Holy, holy, holy” that goes up to the triune Lord. He is pure purity and truth and grace. He is *good in his kindness*, patiently putting up with our waywardness, striving with our rebellious wills, bringing us to life from our death in sin, and then training us for heaven the way a loving nurse brings up a child. How generous, forgiving and tender this patient Spirit of God is! He is *good in what he does*. All his works are good in the highest degree. He suggests good thoughts, prompts good actions, reveals good truths, brings home good promises, helps us reach good attainments and leads us to good results. There’s no spiritual good in all the world that he isn’t the author and sustainer of, and heaven itself will owe the perfect character of its redeemed people to his work. He is *good in every role he fills*. Whether as Comforter, Teacher, Guide, Sanctifier, Life-giver or Intercessor, he does his work well, and every part of it is full of the highest good for God’s church. Those who yield to his influence become good. Those who obey his promptings do good. Those who live under his power receive good.

So let’s treat so good a person as gratitude tells us to. Let’s revere his person and worship him as God over all, blessed forever. Let’s acknowledge his power, and our need of him, by waiting on him in all our holy work. Let’s ask for his help every hour, and never grieve him. And let’s speak in his praise whenever we have the chance. The church will never prosper until it believes in the Holy Spirit more reverently. He is so good and kind that it’s sad indeed that he should be grieved by our slights and neglect.

modern:
Hagar had once found rescue there, and Ishmael had drunk from the water so graciously shown them by the God who lives and sees the sons of men. But that was only a passing visit, the kind worldly people pay the Lord in times of need, when it suits them. They cry to him in trouble but leave him when things go well. Isaac *lived* there, and made the well of the living, all-seeing God his constant source of supply. The usual course of someone’s life, where their soul *lives*, is the true test of their state.

Maybe what happened to Hagar by God’s providence struck Isaac and led him to treat the place with reverence. Its mysterious name made it dear to him. His frequent evening meditations at its edge made him at home by the well. Meeting Rebekah there made his spirit feel at home near the spot. But best of all, he enjoyed fellowship there with the living God, and that’s what made him choose that holy ground for his home.

Let’s learn to live in the presence of the living God. Let’s pray to the Holy Spirit that today and every day we may feel, “Thou God seest me.” May the Lord be like a well to us, delightful, comforting, never failing, springing up to eternal life. The creature’s bottle cracks and dries up, but the Creator’s well never fails. Happy is the one who lives at the well and so has plenty of supplies, always close at hand. The Lord has been a sure helper to others. His name is Shaddai, God All-Sufficient. Our hearts have often had the most delightful fellowship with him. Through him our soul has found her glorious Husband, the Lord Jesus. And in him we live and move and have our being today. So let’s live in the closest fellowship with him. Glorious Lord, hold us so that we never leave you, but live by the well of the living God.

modern: Edom’s princes saw the whole country left empty and counted on an easy conquest. But there was one great obstacle in their way, one they knew nothing about: “*The Lord was there*,” and his presence was the special security of the chosen land. Whatever schemes and plots the enemies of God’s people come up with, the same effective barrier still stands to block them. God’s people are his inheritance. He is among them, and he will protect his own. What comfort this assurance gives us in our troubles and spiritual battles! We’re constantly opposed, and yet constantly kept safe! How often Satan shoots his arrows at our *faith*, but our faith defies the power of hell’s fiery darts. They aren’t only turned aside; they’re put out on its shield, because “the Lord is there.” *Our good works* are attacked by Satan too. No saint has ever had a virtue or a grace that wasn’t a target for hell’s bullets. Whether it was bright, sparkling hope, or warm, eager love, or patience that endures everything, or zeal flaming like coals of fire, the old enemy of everything good has tried to destroy it. The only reason anything good or lovely survives in us is this: “the Lord is there.”

If the Lord is with us through life, we don’t need to worry about our confidence when we die, because *when we come to die*, we’ll find that “the Lord is *there*.” Where the waves are wildest and the water is coldest, we’ll feel the bottom and know that it is good. Our feet will stand on the Rock of Ages when time is passing away. Dear friends, from the start of a Christian’s life to the end, the only reason they don’t perish is that “*the Lord is there*.” When the God of everlasting love changes and leaves his chosen to perish, then the church of God may be destroyed, but not until then, because it’s written, *Jehovah Shammah*, “*The Lord is there*.”

modern:
Perhaps, tested soul, the Lord is doing this to develop your graces. Some of your graces would never be *found* if it weren’t for your trials. Don’t you know that your faith never looks as grand in summer weather as it does in winter? Love is too often like a glowworm, giving little light except in the dark around it. Hope itself is like a star: you can’t see it in the sunshine of good times; you only find it in the night of hard times. Troubles are often the black settings God puts the jewels of his children’s graces in, to make them shine better. Only a little while ago you were on your knees saying, “Lord, I’m afraid I have no faith. Let me know I have faith.” Weren’t you really praying for trials, even if you didn’t realize it? Because how can you know you have faith until your faith is put to work? You can be sure God often sends us trials so that our graces can be found, and we can be sure they’re there.

Besides, it isn’t only finding them. *Real growth* in grace comes from trials God has made holy. God often takes away our comforts and privileges to make us better Christians. He doesn’t train his soldiers in tents of ease and luxury, but by turning them out and getting them used to forced marches and hard service. He makes them wade through streams and swim rivers and climb mountains and walk many a long mile with heavy backpacks of sorrow. Well, Christian, couldn’t this explain the troubles you’re going through? Isn’t the Lord bringing out your graces and making them grow? Isn’t this why he is contending with you?

modern:
It’s quite certain that those whom Christ has washed in his precious blood don’t need to confess their sin as culprits or criminals before God the Judge. In a legal sense Christ has taken away all their sins forever, so that they no longer stand where they can be condemned, but are accepted once for all in the Beloved. But having become children, and offending as children, shouldn’t they go to their heavenly Father every day and confess their sin and admit their wrongdoing as children? Nature teaches that children who do wrong ought to confess to their earthly father, and the grace of God in our hearts teaches us that as Christians we owe the same duty to our heavenly Father. We offend every day, and we shouldn’t rest without being pardoned every day.

Suppose I don’t take my wrongs against my Father to him at once, to be washed away by the cleansing power of the Lord Jesus. What will happen? If I haven’t asked forgiveness and been washed from these offenses against my Father, I’ll feel distant from him. I’ll doubt his love for me. I’ll tremble before him. I’ll be afraid to pray to him. I’ll grow like the prodigal, who was still his father’s child, and yet far away from him. But if, with a child’s sorrow at offending so gracious and loving a Parent, I go to him and tell him everything, and don’t rest until I know I’m forgiven, then I’ll feel a holy love for my Father. I’ll go through my Christian life not only saved, but enjoying peace with God right now through Jesus Christ my Lord.

There’s a wide difference between confessing sin *as a culprit* and confessing sin *as a child*. The Father’s arms are the place for sorrowful confession. We’ve been cleansed once for all, but our feet still need washing from the dirt of our daily walk as children of God.

modern:
Prayer is the forerunner of mercy. Turn to sacred history and you’ll find that hardly ever has a great mercy come to this world without prayer announcing it first. You’ve found this true in your own experience. God has given you many favors you never asked for, but great prayer has still always come before great mercy in your life. When you first found peace through the blood of the cross, you had been praying hard, earnestly pleading with God to take away your doubts and rescue you from your distress. Your assurance came from prayer. Whenever you’ve had high and thrilling joys, you’ve had to see them as answers to your prayers. When you’ve had great rescues from deep trouble and mighty help in great danger, you’ve been able to say, “I sought the Lord, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears.” Prayer is always the introduction to blessing.

It goes before the blessing *like the blessing’s shadow*. When the sunlight of God’s mercies rises on our needs, it throws the shadow of prayer far down across the plain. Or, to use another picture, when God piles up a hill of mercies, he shines from behind them and throws the shadow of prayer over our spirits, so that if we pray much, we can be sure our pleadings are the shadows of mercy. Prayer is also tied to the blessing *to show us its value*. If we had the blessings without asking for them, we’d think them ordinary things, but prayer makes our mercies more precious than diamonds. The things we ask for are precious, but we don’t realize how precious until we’ve sought them earnestly.

notes.note: Asked. God wants his people to ask him for what he has promised.

A humble, earnest request; a prayer.
Not asked for.

modern:
This case is an excellent pattern of all cases where spiritual life is strong. *As soon as someone has found Christ, they start finding others.* I won’t believe you’ve tasted the honey of the gospel if you can eat it all yourself. True grace puts an end to every spiritual monopoly. Andrew *first* found his own brother Simon, and then others. *Family has a very strong claim on our first personal efforts.* Andrew, you did well to begin with Simon. I wonder if there aren’t some Christians handing out tracts at other people’s houses who would do well to hand one out at their own, and some busy with useful work abroad who are neglecting their special place of usefulness at home. You may or may not be called to spread the gospel in some particular area, but you’re certainly called to look after your own servants, your own relatives and friends. Let your faith begin at home. Many tradespeople export their best goods. The Christian shouldn’t. Everywhere they go, their conversation should have the best flavor, but let them make sure to put out the sweetest fruit of spiritual life and witness in their own family.

When Andrew went to find his brother, he had no idea how great Simon would become. As far as we can tell from sacred history, *Simon Peter was worth ten Andrews*, and yet Andrew was the one who brought him to Jesus. You may have very little talent yourself, and yet you may be the means of drawing to Christ someone who will become great in grace and service. Ah, dear friend, you have little idea of the possibilities in you. You may only say a word to a child, and in that child a noble heart may lie asleep that will stir the Christian church in years to come. Andrew has only two talents, but he finds Peter. Go and do the same.

modern: And who comforts like him? Go to some poor, gloomy, distressed child of God. Tell them sweet promises and whisper choice words of comfort in their ear. They’re like the deaf adder that won’t listen to the voice of the charmer, however skillfully he charms. They’re drinking gall and wormwood, and however you comfort them, all you’ll get is a note or two of sad resignation. You won’t draw out any psalms of praise, any hallelujahs, any joyful songs. But let *God* come to his child, let him lift up the light of his face, and the mourner’s eyes shine with hope. Don’t you hear them sing,

You couldn’t have cheered them, but the Lord has done it: “He is the God of all comfort.” There’s no balm in Gilead, but there’s balm in God. There’s no doctor among created things, but the Creator is Jehovah-rophi, the Lord who heals. It’s amazing how one sweet word of God will make whole songs for Christians. One word of God is like a piece of gold, and the Christian is the goldbeater who can hammer out that promise for whole weeks. So, poor Christian, you don’t need to sit down in despair. Go to the Comforter and ask him to give you comfort. You’re a poor dry well. You’ve heard it said that when a pump is dry, you have to pour water down it first, and then you’ll get water. In the same way, Christian, when you’re dry, go to God and ask him to pour his joy into your heart, and then your joy will be full. Don’t go to earthly friends, because you’ll find they’re Job’s comforters after all. Go first and foremost to your “God, that comforteth those that are cast down,” and you’ll soon say, “In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul.”

modern:
A holy character doesn’t keep temptation away: Jesus was tempted. When Satan tempts us, his sparks fall on dry tinder. In Christ’s case it was like striking sparks on water, yet the enemy kept up his evil work. If the devil keeps striking when nothing comes of it, how much more will he do it when he knows how flammable our hearts are! Even if the Holy Spirit makes you very holy, expect the great dog of hell to keep barking at you. In the busy places of life we expect to be tempted, but even being alone won’t protect us from the same trial. Jesus Christ was led away from human company into the wilderness, and he was tempted by the devil. Solitude has its charms and benefits, and it can help to check the lust of the eyes and the pride of life, but the devil will follow us into the loveliest retreats.

Don’t think it’s only worldly people who have dreadful thoughts and blasphemous temptations. Even spiritually minded people go through the same, and in the holiest position we may suffer the darkest temptation. The most complete devotion of spirit won’t insure you against Satan’s temptations. Christ was devoted through and through. It was his food and drink to do the will of the One who sent him, and yet he was tempted! Your hearts may glow with a seraph’s flame of love for Jesus, and still the devil will try to bring you down to Laodicean lukewarmness. If you can tell me when God lets a Christian take off his armor, I’ll tell you when Satan has stopped tempting. Like the old knights in wartime, we must sleep with helmet and breastplate buckled on, because the great deceiver will seize our first unguarded hour to make us his prey. May the Lord keep us watchful at all times, and give us a final escape from the jaw of the lion and the paw of the bear.

modern:
If only we can grasp these words by faith, we have an all-conquering weapon in our hand. What doubt won’t be killed by this two-edged sword? What fear won’t fall with a deadly wound before this arrow from the bow of God’s covenant? Won’t the troubles of life and the pangs of death, the sin inside us and the snares outside, the trials from above and the temptations from below, all seem only light afflictions when we can hide behind the fortress wall of “He hath said”? Yes, whether for delight in our quiet times or for strength in our battles, “He hath said” must be where we turn every day.

This may teach us how extremely valuable it is to *search* the Scriptures. There may be a promise in the Word that fits your case exactly, but you may not know about it, and so you miss its comfort. You’re like prisoners in a dungeon. There may be one key on the ring that would unlock the door and set you free, but if you won’t look for it, you may stay a prisoner, though freedom is so close. There may be a powerful medicine in the great pharmacy of Scripture, and you may stay sick unless you’ll examine and search the Scriptures to find out what “He hath said.” Besides reading the Bible, shouldn’t you store your memory richly with God’s promises? You can remember the sayings of great people. You treasure the lines of famous poets. Shouldn’t you know the words of God deeply, so that you can quote them readily when you need to solve a problem or knock down a doubt? Since “He hath said” is the source of all wisdom and the fountain of all comfort, let it live in you richly, as “A well of water, springing up unto everlasting life.” Then you’ll grow healthy, strong and happy in the life of God.

modern:
We’d be better teachers of others, and less likely to be blown about by every wind of doctrine, if we tried to understand the Word of God more intelligently. Since the Holy Spirit, the Author of the Scriptures, is the only one who can rightly enlighten us to understand them, we should always ask for his teaching and his guidance into all truth. When the prophet Daniel was going to interpret Nebuchadnezzar’s dream, what did he do? He gave himself to earnest prayer that God would open up the vision. The apostle John, in his vision on Patmos, saw a book sealed with seven seals, and no one was found worthy to open it or even to look at it. The book was later opened by the Lion of the tribe of Judah, who had won the right to open it. But first it’s written, “I wept much.” John’s tears were his liquid prayers, and as far as he was concerned, they were the sacred keys that opened the folded book.

So if, for your own good and others’, you want to be “filled with the knowledge of God’s will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding,” remember that prayer is your best way of studying. Like Daniel, you’ll understand the dream and its meaning once you’ve sought God. Like John, you’ll see the seven seals of precious truth broken open after you’ve wept much. Stones aren’t broken except by hard use of the hammer, and the stone breaker has to get down on his knees. Use the hammer of hard work, and exercise the knee of prayer, and there isn’t a stony doctrine in revelation that’s useful for you to understand that won’t fly into pieces under prayer and faith. You can force your way through anything with the leverage of prayer. Thoughts and reasoning are like the steel wedges that get a grip on truth, but prayer is the lever, the crowbar that forces open the iron chest of sacred mystery so we can get at the treasure hidden inside.

modern:
The strength God gives his Josephs is *real* strength. It isn’t boasted bravery, a fiction, something people talk about that ends in smoke. It’s true, *divine strength*. Why does Joseph stand firm against temptation? Because God helps him. There’s nothing we can do without the power of God. All true strength comes from “the mighty God of Jacob.” Notice the *wonderfully personal way* God gives Joseph this strength: “The arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob.” God is pictured putting his hands on Joseph’s hands, laying his arms on Joseph’s arms. As a father teaches his children, so the Lord teaches those who fear him. He puts his arms on theirs. What marvelous condescension! God Almighty, the Eternal, the All-powerful, stoops from his throne and lays his hand on the child’s hand, stretching his arm along Joseph’s arm, so that he will be made strong!

This strength was also covenant strength, because it’s credited to “the mighty *God of Jacob*.” Wherever you read of the God of Jacob in the Bible, you should remember the covenant with Jacob. Christians love to think about God’s covenant. All the power, all the grace, all the blessings, all the mercies, all the comforts, everything we have flows to us from the wellhead, through the covenant. If there were no covenant, we really would fail, because all grace comes from it, as light and heat come from the sun. No angels go up or down except on that ladder Jacob saw, at the top of which stood a covenant God. Christian, it may be that the archers have badly hurt you, shot at you and wounded you, but your bow still stays strong. So be sure to give all the glory to Jacob’s God.

modern:
The Lord “*is slow to anger*.” When mercy comes into the world, she drives winged horses, and her chariot axles glow red-hot with speed. But when anger goes out, it trudges along slowly, because God takes no pleasure in the death of the sinner. God’s rod of mercy is always held out in his hands. His sword of justice is in its sheath, held down by that pierced hand of love that bled for the sins of men. “The Lord is slow to anger” because he is *great in power*. The one who has power over himself is great in power indeed. When God’s power holds itself back, that’s power indeed: the power that restrains the Almighty is almighty power surpassed. A strong-minded person can bear being insulted for a long time, and only resents the wrong when a sense of right demands action. A weak mind is irritated by a little. A strong mind bears it like a rock that doesn’t move, though a thousand breakers crash against it and throw their pitiful malice in spray over its top. God takes note of his enemies, yet he doesn’t stir himself, but holds back his anger. If he were less divine than he is, he would long ago have sent out all his thunders and emptied heaven’s arsenals. He would long ago have blasted the earth with the fearsome fires under its surface, and humanity would have been utterly destroyed. But the greatness of his power brings us mercy.

Dear reader, how are things with you this evening? Can you look to Jesus in humble faith and say, “My Substitute, you are my rock, my trust”? Then, dear friend, don’t be afraid of God’s power. Since by faith you’ve run to Christ for refuge, the power of God doesn’t need to frighten you any more than a warrior’s shield and sword need frighten those he loves. Instead, rejoice that the One who is “great in power” is your Father and Friend.

modern:
No promise is for private use only. Whatever God has said to any one saint, he has said to all. When he opens a well for one, it’s so that all can drink. When he opens a granary door to hand out food, there may be one starving man who’s the reason it’s opened, but all the hungry saints can come and eat too. Whether he gave the word to Abraham or to Moses doesn’t matter, believer. He has given it to you as one of the children of the covenant. There’s no high blessing too lofty for you, no wide mercy too broad for you. Lift up your eyes now to the north and the south, to the east and the west, because all this is yours. Climb to the top of Pisgah and look out to the farthest edge of God’s promise, because the land is all your own. There’s no brook of living water you can’t drink from. If the land flows with milk and honey, eat the honey and drink the milk, because both are yours. Be bold to believe, for he has said, “I will never leave *thee*, nor forsake *thee*.”

In this promise God gives his people everything. “*I* will never leave thee.” Then none of God’s qualities can ever stop working for us. Is he mighty? He’ll show himself strong for those who trust him. Is he love? Then he’ll have mercy on us with lovingkindness. Whatever qualities make up the character of God, every one of them, to its fullest extent, will be at work on our side. To put it all in one: there’s nothing you can want, nothing you can ask for, nothing you can need in time or eternity, nothing living, nothing dying, nothing in this world, nothing in the next, nothing now, nothing on the morning of the resurrection, nothing in heaven, that isn’t contained in this text: “I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.”
