modern: You don’t get to make your own cross, though unbelief is a master carpenter at making crosses. Nor are you allowed to choose your own cross, though self-will would love to be lord and master. Your cross is prepared and appointed for you by God’s love, and you’re to accept it cheerfully. You’re to take up the cross as your chosen badge and burden, not stand there finding fault with it. Tonight Jesus tells you to put your shoulder under his easy yoke. Don’t kick against it in a temper, or trample on it in vanity, or fall under it in despair, or run away from it in fear. Take it up like a true follower of Jesus. Jesus carried a cross; he leads the way on the path of sorrow. Surely you couldn’t want a better guide! And if he carried a cross, what nobler burden could you want? The *Via Crucis*, the way of the cross, is the way of safety. Don’t be afraid to walk its thorny paths.

Dear friends, the cross isn’t made of feathers or lined with velvet. It’s heavy, and it chafes disobedient shoulders. But it isn’t an iron cross, though your fears have painted it the color of iron. It’s a wooden cross, and a man can carry it, because the Man of Sorrows tried the load. Take up your cross, and by the power of the Spirit of God you’ll soon love it so much that, like Moses, you wouldn’t trade the reproach of Christ for all the treasures of Egypt. Remember that Jesus carried it, and it will smell sweet. Remember that it will soon be followed by the crown, and the thought of the coming weight of glory will greatly lighten the present heaviness of trouble. The Lord help you to bow your spirit in surrender to God’s will before you fall asleep tonight, so that when you wake with tomorrow’s sun, you’ll go out to the day’s cross with the holy, yielded spirit that suits a follower of the Crucified One.

modern:
Here is *sovereign mercy*: “I will give them the shower in its season.” Isn’t it sovereign, *divine* mercy? Because who can say, “I will give them showers,” except God? There’s only one voice that can speak to the clouds and tell them to bring rain. Who sends rain on the earth? Who scatters the showers on the green grass? Don’t I, the Lord? In the same way, grace is the gift of God, and people can’t create it.

It’s also *needed* grace. What would the ground do without showers? You can break up the clods and sow your seed, but what can you do without rain? God’s blessing is just as absolutely necessary. You work in vain until God gives the plentiful shower and sends salvation down.

Then it’s *plentiful grace*. “I will send them showers.” It doesn’t say, “I will send them drops,” but “showers.” It’s the same with grace. When God gives a blessing, he usually gives it in such measure that there isn’t room enough to receive it. Plentiful grace! Ah, we need plentiful grace to keep us humble, to make us prayerful, to make us holy; plentiful grace to make us zealous, to keep us through this life, and at last to land us in heaven. We can’t do without soaking showers of grace.

Again, it’s *timely grace*. “I will cause the shower to come down *in his season*.” What’s your season this morning? Is it a season of drought? Then that’s the season for showers. Is it a season of great heaviness and black clouds? Then that’s the season for showers. “As thy days so shall thy strength be.”

And here is a *varied* blessing. “I will give thee *showers* of blessing.” The word is plural. God will send blessings of every kind. All God’s blessings go together, like the links of a golden chain. If he gives grace to turn you to him, he’ll also give grace to comfort you. He’ll send “showers of blessing.” Look up today, parched plant, and open your leaves and flowers for a heavenly watering.

modern:
What a sweet answer to an anxious question! Tonight let’s rejoice in it. Zion, there are good things in store for you. Your time of labor pains will soon be over. Your children will be born. Your captivity will end. Bear the rod patiently for a while, and in the darkness keep trusting God, because his love burns toward you. God loves the church with a love too deep for human imagination. He loves her with all his infinite heart. So let her children take courage. She can’t be far from prosperity when God speaks to her “good words and comfortable words.”

The prophet goes on to tell us what these comforting words are: “I am jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy.” The Lord loves his church so much that he can’t bear her to go astray after others. And when she has, he can’t bear her to suffer too much or too heavily. He won’t let his enemies afflict her; he is displeased with them because they add to her misery. When God seems most to have left his church, his heart is warm toward her. History shows that whenever God uses a rod to discipline his servants, he always breaks it afterward, as if he hated the rod that gave his children pain. “Like as a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth them that fear him.” God hasn’t forgotten us because he strikes us; his blows are no proof that he doesn’t love us.

If this is true of his church *as a whole*, it must also be true of *each individual member*. You may be afraid the Lord has passed you by, but he hasn’t. The One who counts the stars and calls them by name is in no danger of forgetting his own children. He knows your case as thoroughly as if you were the only creature he ever made, or the only saint he ever loved. Come to him and be at peace.

modern:
It’s pleasant to walk across the countryside after a storm has blown itself out, to smell the freshness of the plants after the rain has gone, and to see the drops glistening like the purest diamonds in the sunlight. That’s the Christian’s position. He’s walking through a land where the storm has spent itself on his Savior’s head. If a few drops of sorrow are still falling, they fall from clouds of mercy, and Jesus cheers him with the assurance that they aren’t there to destroy him.

But how terrible it is to watch a storm approaching: to see the warning signs, to see the birds of the air droop their wings, to see the cattle lower their heads in terror, to see the sky turn black, and to look for the sun that no longer shines and at the heavens angry and frowning! How terrible to wait for a hurricane to arrive, the kind that sometimes strikes in the tropics, waiting in dreadful suspense for the wind to break loose in fury, tearing trees up by the roots, knocking rocks off their bases and hurling down every house people live in!

And yet, sinner, that’s where you are right now. No hot drops have fallen yet, but a shower of fire is coming. No terrible winds are howling around you yet, but God’s storm is gathering its dreadful artillery. For now the floodwaters are held back by mercy, but the floodgates will soon be opened. God’s thunderbolts are still in his storehouse, but look, the storm is hurrying on, and how dreadful that moment will be when God, robed in vengeance, marches out in fury! Where, where, where, sinner, will you hide your head? Where will you run? Oh, that the hand of mercy would lead you to Christ now! He is freely offered to you in the gospel. His pierced side is the rock of shelter. You know you need him. Believe in him, throw yourself on him, and then the fury will be over and past for you forever.

modern:
Instead of going to Nineveh to preach the Word, as God told him, Jonah disliked the job and went down to Joppa to get away from it. There are times when God’s servants shrink back from duty. But what comes of it? What did Jonah lose by what he did?

*He lost the presence and comforting enjoyment of God’s love.* When we serve our Lord Jesus as believers should, our God is with us, and even if the whole world is against us, what does it matter if God is with us? But the moment we draw back and follow our own ideas, we’re at sea without a pilot. Then we may bitterly grieve and groan, “O my God, where have you gone? How could I have been so foolish as to avoid your service, and lose all the bright shining of your face this way? This is too high a price. Let me come back to my loyalty, so that I can rejoice in your presence.”

Next, Jonah *lost all peace of mind*. Sin soon destroys a believer’s comfort. It’s the poisonous upas tree, whose leaves drip deadly drops that kill the life of joy and peace.

Jonah also *lost everything he could have drawn on for comfort in any other situation*. He couldn’t plead God’s promise of protection, because he wasn’t in God’s ways. He couldn’t say, “Lord, I’m running into these difficulties while doing my duty, so help me through them.” He was reaping what he had sown, filled with his own ways. Christian, don’t play the Jonah, unless you want all the waves and the breakers rolling over your head. You’ll find in the long run that it’s far harder to avoid God’s work and will than to give yourself to it at once.

And *Jonah lost his time*, because he had to go to Nineveh after all. It’s hard to fight against God. Let’s give in to him at once.

modern:
Salvation is the work of God. He alone brings to life the soul that is “dead in trespasses and sins,” and he is also the one who keeps that soul alive spiritually. He is both “Alpha and Omega.” “Salvation is of the Lord.” If I’m prayerful, God makes me prayerful. If I have graces, they’re God’s gifts to me. If I keep going in a consistent life, it’s because he holds me up with his hand. I do nothing at all toward keeping myself safe except what God first does in me. Whatever I have, all my goodness, is from the Lord alone. Where I sin, that’s my own doing, but where I do right, that’s God’s, wholly and completely. If I’ve driven off a spiritual enemy, it was the Lord’s strength that steeled my arm. Do I live a life given to God in front of others? It isn’t I, but Christ who lives in me. Am I being made holy? I didn’t clean myself up; God’s Holy Spirit makes me holy. Am I being weaned from the world? I’m weaned by *God’s* discipline, made holy for my good. Am I growing in knowledge? The great Teacher is teaching me. All my jewels were crafted by heavenly skill.

I find in God everything I need, but in myself I find nothing but sin and misery. “He only is my rock and my salvation.” Do I feed on the Word? That Word would be no food for me unless the Lord made it food for my soul and helped me feed on it. Do I live on the manna that comes down from heaven? What is that manna but Jesus Christ himself, come in the flesh, whose body and blood I eat and drink? Am I constantly receiving fresh strength? Where do I gather my might? My help comes from heaven’s hills: without Jesus I can do nothing. As a branch can’t bear fruit unless it stays in the vine, neither can I unless I stay in him. What Jonah learned in the great deep, let me learn this morning in my prayer room: “Salvation is of the Lord.”

modern:
This rule seems strange enough, yet there was wisdom in it, because a disease that had come right out to the surface showed that the body underneath was sound. This evening it may be good for us to see what this unusual rule pictures. We’re lepers too, and we can read the leper’s law as applying to ourselves. When someone sees that they’re completely lost and ruined, covered all over with the stain of sin, with no part free from pollution; when they disown any righteousness of their own and plead guilty before the Lord, then they’re clean through the blood of Jesus and the grace of God. Hidden, unfelt, unconfessed sin is the real leprosy. But when sin is seen and felt, it has received its deathblow, and the Lord looks with eyes of mercy on the soul that suffers from it. Nothing is more deadly than self-righteousness, and nothing more hopeful than a broken heart.

We must confess that we are “nothing else but sin,” because no confession short of that will be the whole truth. And if the Holy Spirit is at work in us, convincing us of sin, we’ll have no trouble saying it; it will come from our lips of its own accord. What comfort this text gives truly awakened sinners! The very thing that so badly discouraged them is turned here into a sign and symptom of hope. Stripping comes before clothing. Digging out the foundation is the first thing in building. And a thorough sense of sin is one of the earliest works of grace in the heart. Poor leprous sinner, without one healthy spot, take heart from this text, and come to Jesus just as you are:

modern:
The Israelites in the wilderness *were always facing change*. Whenever the pillar stopped moving, the tents were pitched. But the next day, before the morning sun had risen, the trumpet sounded, the ark was on the move, and the pillar of fire and cloud was leading the way through narrow mountain passes, up the hillside or across the dry wasteland of the wilderness. They had hardly any time to rest before they heard, “Away! This isn’t your rest. You must keep journeying on toward Canaan!” They were never long in one place. Even wells and palm trees couldn’t keep them. Yet they had a lasting home in their God. His pillar of cloud was the roof over their heads, and its flame at night was their household fire. They had to keep moving from place to place, always changing, never with time to settle down and say, “Now we’re secure; this is where we’ll live.” “Yet,” says Moses, “though we’re always changing, Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations.”

The Christian knows no change in his relationship with God. He may be rich today and poor tomorrow. He may be sick today and well tomorrow. He may be happy today, and tomorrow he may be in distress. But there’s no change in his relationship to God. If he loved me yesterday, he loves me today. My unmoving home of rest is my blessed Lord. Let prospects be ruined, let hopes be blasted, let joy wither, let mildew destroy everything: I’ve lost nothing of what I have in God. He is “my strong habitation whereunto I can continually resort.” I’m a pilgrim in the world, but at home in my God. On earth I wander, but in God I live in a quiet home.

modern:
The Lord Jesus went out on behalf of his people *as their representative before the throne, long before they appeared on the stage of time*. It was “from everlasting” that he signed the agreement with his Father to pay blood for blood, suffering for suffering, agony for agony and death for death on behalf of his people. It was “from everlasting” that he gave himself up without a word of complaint, so that from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot he might sweat great drops of blood, and be spat on, pierced, mocked, torn apart and crushed under the pains of death. His goings forth as our Guarantor were from everlasting.

Stop, my soul, and wonder! You’ve had goings forth in the person of Jesus “from everlasting.” Christ didn’t only love you when you were born into the world. His delight was in the sons of men before there were any sons of men. He thought of them often. From everlasting to everlasting he had set his affection on them. What, my soul! Has he been so long at work on your salvation, and won’t he finish it? Has he been going out from everlasting to save me, and will he lose me now? What! Has he carried me in his hand like a precious jewel, and will he now let me slip through his fingers? Did he choose me before the mountains were formed or the channels of the deep were dug, and will he reject me now? Impossible! I’m sure he wouldn’t have loved me so long if he weren’t a Lover who never changes. If he could grow tired of me, he’d have grown tired of me long ago. If he hadn’t loved me with a love as deep as hell and as strong as death, he’d have turned from me long ago. Oh, joy above all joys, to know that I’m his everlasting inheritance, which can never be taken away, given to him by his Father before the earth existed! Everlasting love will be the pillow for my head tonight.

modern:
It’s the believer’s privilege to use these words. If he’s looking for anything from the world, it’s a poor “expectation” indeed. But if he looks to God to supply his needs, whether in earthly or spiritual blessings, his “expectation” won’t be in vain. He can draw on the bank of faith again and again and have his needs supplied out of the riches of God’s lovingkindness. I know this much: I’d rather have God for my banker than all the Rothschilds. My Lord never fails to honor his promises, and when we bring them to his throne, he never sends them back unanswered. So I’ll wait only at his door, because he always opens it with the hand of generous grace. I’ll try him again this very hour.

But we have “expectations” beyond this life. We’ll soon die, and then our “expectation is from him.” Don’t we expect that when we lie on our sickbed, he’ll send angels to carry us to his arms? We believe that when the pulse is faint and the heart heaves heavily, some angel messenger will stand and look at us with loving eyes and whisper, “Sister spirit, come away!” As we come near heaven’s gate, we expect to hear the welcome invitation, “Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” We’re expecting harps of gold and crowns of glory. We hope soon to be among the crowd of shining ones before the throne. We’re looking forward to and longing for the time when we’ll be like our glorious Lord, for “We shall see him as he is.” So if these are your “expectations,” my soul, live for God. Live with the desire and the resolve to glorify the One all your supplies come from, by whose grace in choosing, redeeming and calling you, you have any “expectation” of glory to come.

modern:
See the faithfulness of God’s love. Notice that this woman had daily needs. She had herself and her son to feed in a time of famine, and now, on top of that, the prophet Elijah had to be fed too. But though the need was three times as great, the flour didn’t run out, because she had a *constant supply*. Every day she dipped into the barrel, and yet every day it stayed the same. You, dear reader, have daily needs, and because they come so often, you tend to fear that the barrel of flour will be empty one day and the jar of oil will fail you. You can be sure that, as the Word of God says, it won’t happen. Each day may bring its trouble, but it will also bring its help. And even if you live longer than Methuselah, and your needs are as many as the sands on the seashore, God’s grace and mercy will last through every need, and you’ll never know real lack.

For three long years in this widow’s time, the sky never saw a cloud, and the stars never shed a holy tear of dew on the wicked earth. Famine and ruin and death turned the land into a howling wilderness, but this woman was never hungry, but always happy in plenty. It will be the same for you. You’ll see the sinner’s hope perish, because he trusts his own strength. You’ll see the proud Pharisee’s confidence totter, because he builds his hope on sand. You’ll even see your own plans blasted and withered. But you yourself will find that your fortress is a stronghold of rock: “Your bread shall be given you, and your water shall be sure.” Better to have God as your guardian than the Bank of England as your property. You could spend all the wealth of the Indies, but you can never use up the infinite riches of God.

modern: The thunder of the law and the terrors of judgment are all used to bring us to Christ, but the final victory is won by lovingkindness. The prodigal set out for his father’s house because he was in need. But his father saw him a long way off and ran to meet him, so that the last steps he took toward his father’s house were taken with the kiss still warm on his cheek and the welcome still ringing like music in his ears.

The Master came to the door one night and knocked with the iron hand of the law. The door shook and trembled on its hinges, but the man piled every piece of furniture he could find against it, saying, “I won’t let him in.” The Master turned away. But before long he came back, and with his own soft hand, using mostly the part where the nail had gone through, he knocked again, oh, so softly and tenderly. This time the door didn’t shake, but strange to say, it opened, and there on his knees was the once unwilling host, rejoicing to welcome his guest. “Come in, come in. You’ve knocked in such a way that my heart is moved for you. I couldn’t bear to think of your pierced hand leaving its bloodstain on my door, and of you going away homeless, ‘Thy head filled with dew, and thy locks with the drops of the night.’ I give in, I give in; your love has won my heart.” It’s the same in every case: lovingkindness wins the day. What Moses with the tablets of stone could never do, Christ does with his pierced hand. That’s the teaching of effectual calling. Do I understand it from my own experience? Can I say, “He drew me, and I followed on, glad to confess the voice divine”? If so, may he keep on drawing me, until at last I sit down at the marriage supper of the Lamb.

modern:
Dear reader, have you received the spirit which is of God, worked in your soul by the Holy Spirit? You can see clearly how necessary the Holy Spirit’s work in the heart is from this fact: *everything God the Father and God the Son have done must be useless to us unless the Spirit reveals these things to our souls*. What effect does the teaching of election have on anyone until the Spirit of God enters them? Election is a dead letter to me until the Spirit of God calls me out of darkness into his marvelous light. *Then*, through my calling, I see my election, and knowing God has called me, I know I was chosen in his eternal purpose. A covenant was made with the Lord Jesus Christ by his Father, but what good is that covenant to us until the Holy Spirit brings us its blessings and opens our hearts to receive them? There the blessings hang on the nail, Christ Jesus, but we’re too short to reach them. The Spirit of God takes them down and hands them to us, and so they actually become ours.

The blessings of the covenant in themselves are like the manna in the sky, far out of human reach. But the Spirit of God opens the windows of heaven and scatters the living bread around the camp of the spiritual Israel. Christ’s finished work is like wine stored in the vat; because of unbelief we can neither draw it nor drink it. The Holy Spirit dips our cup into this precious wine, and then we drink. But without the Spirit we’re as truly dead in sin as if the Father had never chosen us and the Son had never bought us with his blood. The Holy Spirit is absolutely necessary to our well-being. Let’s walk lovingly toward him, and tremble at the thought of grieving him.
